chore(release): pre-skip already-published packages in changeset publish (#712)

The Release workflow runs on every push to master. Under tokenless OIDC +
pnpm, changeset publish's pre-publish check misreads the registry and
re-attempts an already-live version; npm's E403 arrives in pnpm's
{ code, message } shape, which crashes @changesets/cli with an unguarded
undefined.includes(...) TypeError inside isAlreadyPublishedError. The crash
exits non-zero with no per-package error lines, so the wrapper's text-match
swallow could not recognize it: the publish step went red, published was
never set, and the GitHub-release step was skipped -- stranding
@vuetify/v0@1.0.1 on npm with no v1.0.1 release (changesets #2099 / #2184).

Pre-skip the crash instead of classifying it after the fact: any non-private
workspace package whose current version is already on npm is temporarily
marked private on disk (CI-only, always restored) so changeset publish skips
it and never re-attempts the publish. Genuinely-new versions still publish
and print their New tag: lines, so the changesets action's outputs and the
release steps fire as before.

Adds a null-safe fallback swallow for the crash signature (non-zero exit with
no parseable error lines) when the registry confirms every intended version
is live -- never fabricating New tag: lines, so a clean skip leaves published
false rather than looping the release step on a no-op.

chore(bench): host calibration anchors so metrics survive GHA runner rotation (#716)

* chore(bench): host calibration anchors so metrics survive GHA runner rotation

`runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` pins the OS image, not the CPU. GHA rotates hosts
across generations differing ~1.5x in single-thread throughput, so identical
code benched on two runners yields two different sets of absolute ops/s.

PR #714 is the worked example: re-benching the byte-identical 1.0.0 npm dist
moved +50.9% median across 623 benches, put 582 of them outside the ±20%
canary band, and flipped 35 tier badges. Node (.nvmrc 26.0.0), vitest, and
packages/0/src were all provably unchanged across the two runs.

Adds a fixed 13-anchor suite spanning ~100ns-1ms that imports nothing from v0,
and records the trimmed geometric mean of `anchors / stored baseline` as
`apparatus.scale` in benchmarks.json, metrics.json, and every per-version
snapshot, alongside a CPU/node/pnpm/runner fingerprint. Artifacts keep raw hz;
consumers divide by scale, so raw stays recoverable as `hz * scale`.

Measured on the #714 pair: whole-suite bias drops +49.3% -> +1.5%, and the five
canaries fall from +44..+61% (all flagged) to -1.9..+9.6% (none flagged).

`BASELINE_ANCHOR_HZ` is null until a maintainer captures it from a CI run, so
scale is 1 and this changes no committed number today. calibration.test.ts
hashes the anchor file and blocks the silent re-baseline that editing an anchor
would otherwise cause.

Does not fix host-*shape* sensitivity: ~6% of benches (createTokens alias
resolution moves ~2.5x vs the suite's 1.47x) survive normalization as real
outliers and still need quarantining.

* chore(bench): move anchors out of packages/0/src and use v0 isNumber in docs

Two review fixes.

The anchor suite sat at packages/0/src/__bench__/, which made every tool that
reads `packages/<name>/src/` as "shipped source" misclassify apparatus as a
library change — changeset-reminder.js:21 matches exactly that pattern, which is
why the bot asked for a changeset on a file that never enters dist. Moved to
packages/0/bench/. Content is unchanged, so the guard hash still matches.

src/ was only ever chosen because normalizeFilepath anchored on
`packages/0/src/`; anything outside it kept its absolute path and tripped the
local-path guard. Generalized the marker to `packages/0/`, which returns a
byte-identical string for src files (the marker only sets where the slice
starts) so existing artifact keys are untouched, and correctly normalizes
packages/0/bench/ from both CI and local checkouts.

Also scoped the rule doc to the new path so it still auto-loads when someone
edits the anchors — that is precisely when the do-not-edit contract needs
reading — and noted there that the anchors are exempt from the per-bench-file
standards (fixture isolation, 1K/10K, category comments), since they describe
the machine rather than v0.

Type guards: useAsk.ts and useBenchmarkData.ts now use `isNumber` from
@vuetify/v0, matching useBenchmarkHistory.ts:98. The four duplicated scale reads
in scripts/ collapsed to one — generate-metrics.js and generate-metrics-history
now call scaleOf() instead of re-deriving it, leaving scaleOf and extractAnchors
as the only raw checks. Those two cannot use isNumber: it lives in
utilities/helpers.ts, which imports `vue` and the `#v0/constants/globals` alias
that scripts/tsconfig.json has no path for, and these scripts run unbundled
under node.

chore(bench): collapse generated metrics artifacts in diffs (#717)

The metrics pipeline writes 300-450KB of pretty-printed JSON per artifact, and
`metrics:history --force` rewrites every per-version snapshot on each release.
#714 was 30,060 additions / 20,087 deletions for a single added version.

Nobody reviews a 50k-line diff, which means the "close this PR to discard if the
delta looks like runner noise" instruction in the auto-PR body was unactionable —
the noise it asks you to spot is precisely what the diff size hides.

Marking these linguist-generated collapses them on GitHub and drops them from
language stats; -diff stops git generating a textual diff at all. Verified: a
mutated metrics.json now reports `Bin 340481 -> 342479 bytes, 0 insertions(+),
0 deletions(-)` instead of thousands of lines. Artifact comparison should go
through scripts/report-benchmark-delta.ts regardless, since raw ops/s are not
comparable across hosts.

Also documents why a global `* text=auto` must never be added here: the sha256
guard in packages/0/bench/calibration.test.ts exists to stop a silent
re-baseline of the entire benchmark history, and line-ending normalization would
make it pass on some platforms and fail on others.

fix(useResizeObserver): surface borderBoxSize and contentBoxSize on entries (#725)

* fix(useResizeObserver): surface borderBoxSize and contentBoxSize on entries

useResizeObserver forwarded the `box` option to ResizeObserver.observe() but
narrowed every reported entry down to contentRect + target, discarding the
native borderBoxSize / contentBoxSize. `box: 'border-box'` therefore changed
only *when* the callback fired, never *what* it measured — an element with
padding or a border measured short by exactly that amount, silently.

Both size arrays are now forwarded to the callback, mirroring the native
entry shape (one entry per box fragment). They are populated regardless of
`box`, matching the platform.

The `immediate` synthesis has to produce the same fields, so it now derives
both boxes from getComputedStyle instead of a lone getBoundingClientRect.
Resolved width/height follow `box-sizing`, so the derivation branches on it;
logical axes swap under vertical writing modes. Every read tolerates a
partial style declaration — Avatar's browser test stubs getComputedStyle
down to two properties, and elements with no layout box resolve to ''.

contentRect keeps its existing client-rect source in both paths, so callers
that don't read the new fields are unaffected.

Closes #724

* test(useResizeObserver): cover every box-model branch in the unit project

CI measures .ts coverage from the unit project only (pr-checks.yml runs
--project '!v0:browser' --coverage.include='packages/0/src/**/*.ts'; the
browser job is scoped to components/**/*.vue). The browser test therefore
contributed nothing to patch coverage, leaving the box-sizing, writing-mode,
and numeric-fallback branches of the immediate synthesis unhit.

Drive each branch from happy-dom by stubbing getComputedStyle: border-box vs
content-box derivation, vertical writing mode, a non-numeric resolved length
falling back to the client rect, a partial style declaration, and the content
box clamped at zero. Real-layout verification of the same math stays in the
browser test, which happy-dom can't do.

Also renames the module-local px() to pxToNumber() — it takes "16px" and
returns 16, matching the <source>To<target> convention of hexToRgb / rgbToHex
rather than the to<Target> normalizers.

fix(useProxyModel): hold a model value whose ticket has not registered (#727)

Setting the model to a value with no registered ticket left it unselected —
correct, since the ticket resolves it later via onRegister — but the same tick
then wrote the context's current selection back over the model. That discarded
the caller's intent before registration could happen.

Where the model is a writable computed, the write-back also ran the setter,
producing a real state change that echoed back as a fresh model change and
cleared the pending set, so the late-registering ticket never resolved.

Pending values are now distinguished from rejected ones using the registry's
value reverse-lookup: a value with no ticket is held, while a value whose
ticket exists but was refused (disabled, mandatory) still reverts.

fix(useProxyModel): accept contexts that narrow browse's value type (#728)

ProxyModelTarget declared browse as a property taking `unknown`. Under
strictFunctionTypes a function-typed property is checked contravariantly, so
any context narrowing its ticket value — ProgressContext and SliderContext
both key theirs on a ShallowRef<number> — no longer satisfied the interface
and typecheck broke on master.

Method shorthand would give bivariant parameters, but the repo forbids it
(@typescript-eslint/method-signature-style). `never` accepts every concrete
browse instead, and the single call site widens with an explicit cast, so the
unsoundness stays where it actually happens rather than in the contract.

Also names the return type ID, matching createRegistry's own browse.

Both jobs now report the full include set from the root config and Codecov

fix(utilities): preserve element types, tuples and readonly in isArray narrowing (#745)

* fix(utilities): preserve element types, tuples and readonly in isArray narrowing

isArray narrowed every input to `unknown[]`, which erased the element
type of arrays whose elements involve `any`, turned `readonly` array
unions into an intersection that is not an array of anything, and left
the array constituent in place in the negative branch.

Narrow via `Extract<T, readonly unknown[]>` so array constituents pass
through untouched, with an `any` branch matching `Array.isArray` and an
`unknown[]` fallback that reproduces the previous narrowing. `NoInfer<T[]>`
admits the `any` branch past the predicate-assignability check without
letting an array argument capture the inference site.

Measured against 87 converted `Array.isArray` call sites in vuetify core
on refactor/v0-type-guards: 6 errors before, 1 after — and that one is a
real readonly variance bug in core that both the old guard and the
built-in were hiding.

test: add advisory axe-core accessibility sweep for every component (#736)

* test: add advisory axe-core accessibility sweep for every component (#732)

35 of 171 test files assert `aria-*` by hand. That is real coverage and it is
not the gap — every one of those assertions is an attribute someone thought to
check. Nothing audits the ones nobody thought of, which is how the open a11y
batch (#608, #611-#616) survived a suite those 35 files already passed.

Adds a sweep that mounts each of the 40 shipped components in the shape its own
`@example` JSDoc documents, in the `v0:browser` project's real Chromium, and
hands it to axe-core. Advisory: violations are collected and reported, never
asserted. Gating on day one buys either a red master or suppressions written to
deadline, and a suppression written to get CI green is a permanently invisible
violation.

First pass: 10 violations, 13 elements, 7 components, 8 rules. Three reproduce
open issues (#608 via Progress, #613 via Selection and Select). The other five
are new. Full breakdown in the PR body; not fixed here.

Uses axe-core directly rather than `vitest-axe`, which issue #732 proposed and
the accessibility guide recommends to users. `vitest-axe` reaches for
`node:module` at import time and fails to load in Vitest browser mode at both
0.1.0 and 1.0.0-pre.5 — it is a jsdom/happy-dom tool. axe-core is the engine
underneath it either way. The guide now says so.

The manifest check derives its expected set from maturity.json rather than from
this file, so promoting a component out of `draft` without writing it a fixture
fails the sweep.

CI runs it as a separate `a11y` job with `continue-on-error: true`, mirroring
the existing `vapor` job's non-blocking-signal pattern, and tees the breakdown
into the GitHub step summary. Flipping to a gate is deleting that one line.

* test: audit degenerate component shapes in the accessibility sweep

The canonical sweep audits each component in the shape its own `@example`
documents, and a documented example is written by someone thinking about the
example. The failure mode that ships is the omission — the optional
sub-component nobody mounted, the optional prop nobody passed.

Adds `fixtures/degenerate/`: 11 fixtures, each the canonical shape with one
documented-optional part removed and nothing else changed. Membership rule is
stated at the map so it does not drift into a grab bag; components whose
canonical fixture already omits its optional name (NumberField, Progress,
Rating, Select, Slider) are absent because they are already in the first-pass
count.

Counted and reported separately from the canonical number, which is unchanged

at 2, 0.615% at 3, 0.565% at 4. A trim of 1 was too narrow because this host

* chore(bench): close six holes in the host guard found by second-model review

Codex and Grok reviewed the apparatus; all six findings reproduced against
source or on the reference host.

1. The guard was blind to single-core contention. It sampled only the
   aggregate /proc/stat line, and one saturated core on a 36-thread host is
   2.8% of total CPU -- under any sane whole-machine threshold, while being
   the likeliest real contention there is. Reproduced: one busy thread read
   2.8% and sailed through. Now samples per-CPU too and blocks above 35% on
   any single one, a limit set from the measured gap between an idle box
   (0-1% on its busiest core) and a real workload (100%).

2. Governor restore was unsound for any original but powersave. readGovernor
   can return schedutil, ondemand or mixed(...), which the helper rejects,
   so the cast to its two-value API failed at runtime and left the desktop
   pinned to performance -- the exact outcome the comment promised to
   prevent. The hold now declines to touch an unrestorable governor at all.

3. mkdtempSync sat between setting the governor and the try block, so a
   throw there leaked performance. Everything fallible now happens first.

4. finally does not run on Ctrl-C. Release is now bound to SIGINT/SIGTERM --
   which by itself did nothing, because handlers only run when the event
   loop turns and execFileSync blocked it for the whole suite. Verified:
   SIGINT left vitest benching on and the box on performance, the interrupt
   queued behind the run it was meant to abort. runOnce now spawns async and
   the handler kills the child; re-verified, the box comes back to powersave.

5. Skipping the guard on CI=true disabled it on the machine it was written
   for, since the reference host under automation sets CI too. Ephemeral is
   now read as CI set AND no governor helper present. The host is always
   inspected regardless, so apparatus.env records conditions behind every
   artifact even when nothing would be stopped.

6. iowait was counted as idle. A disk-bound neighbour still moves memory
   bandwidth, evicts page cache and raises interrupt load. Verified: a dd
   loop read 2.9% aggregate -- invisible -- and 38.4% on one core.

apparatus.env gains peak, the busiest-core figure, which is the load-bearing

* chore(bench): re-baseline from four runs, and record what normalization is worth

The baseline was captured from a single median-of-3 run, so that run's noise
became the unit. It is now the per-anchor median across four independent
full-suite runs on the idle reference host.

Medianing was necessary but not sufficient, and the measurement that came
out of it matters more than the new numbers. Across those four runs, three
produced a scale within 0.4% of 1 while the fourth produced 0.963: its
allocation-heavy anchors collapsed (object churn -38%, grouped aggregate
-27%) while the 446 real benches moved only +1.4%. The median anchor moved
-4.6%, so no trim setting rescues it -- the anchors did not track the suite
that run. Normalizing by that scale would have injected ~4% of error into
every bench rather than removing any.

Ruled out as a cause: the async spawn change landed between runs, but a
fourth run on the new code behaved normally (scale 0.9957), so the outlier
is a property of the anchors and not of the harness.

The honest reading is that on an unchanged host this apparatus is a no-op
two runs in three and a ~4% distortion in the third. Its value is cross-host
-- insurance against a future CPU, kernel or Node major -- and since every
artifact stores its raw anchors, that correction stays derivable after the
fact. Both the code and the rules doc now say so, and say to read a sub-5%
normalized delta as noise.

* chore(bench): delete host calibration, keep the fixed host

The calibration apparatus corrected for GHA rotating CPUs between runs. That
problem was solved by moving to a fixed workstation; what remained was a
correction for a variable that no longer varies. Measured on four full-suite
runs of identical code, it was not merely redundant but harmful:

  method              per-bench med   per-feature med   per-feature worst
  raw ops/s                   1.81%             2.16%               4.96%
  anchor-normalized           3.53%             6.23%               9.50%

Dividing by the scale roughly tripled the disagreement between measurements
of identical code. On one of the four runs the anchors moved -4.6% at the
median while the 446 real benches moved +1.4%: the probe did not track the
workload it was correcting, so its correction was injected error. No trim
setting rescues a wrong central tendency. The least reproducible file in the
whole suite was calibration.bench.ts itself, 9.42% against a worst real
feature of 4.96%.

Two facts made this safe and settled. Every committed artifact carried
scale: 1 -- the apparatus was inert its whole life, so nothing published
changes and there is no migration. And of ~35 comparable projects surveyed
(V8, Speedometer, Node core, ts-perf, rustc-perf, LNT, SPEC, JMH, benchstat,
criterion, Vue core, Deno, Bun, esbuild, tinybench, CodSpeed, ...) zero
derive a host scale from a synthetic probe and divide by it. Benchmark.js
shipped exactly this and removed it for exactly this reason.

Deleted: calibration.bench.ts (13 frozen anchors and the never-edit-this
hazard around them), calibration.test.ts, scripts/lib/calibration.ts,

Kept, because recording beats correcting: the env fingerprint moves to

suite moved between two artifacts, so host-wide movement is visible in one
line rather than silently folded into every figure.

that this setup is trustworthy is checkable rather than asserted: it measures
identical code repeatedly and fails if the results disagree by more than the
apparatus allows. Thresholds are set from measured behaviour, not taste.

The per-run governor toggle rested on a single measurement: median CV 1.79%

to track the suite it was meant to describe. The evidence for the toggle was
void the moment the anchors were.

granting the bench account passwordless access to it, restore-on-signal
plumbing, and a failure mode where an unrestorable governor could strand a
desktop at max clocks. For an effect no longer credibly measured at all.

* docs: describe the tier system that actually exists

averaging is precisely what it exists to avoid, since one flattering
microbench would mask a slow path.

* feat(emerald): add the icon system — EmIcon + role tokens

Emerald draws its own glyphs from a role vocabulary instead of leaving
each site to inline its own SVG. src/icons.ts holds 48 canonical roles as
24x24 stroke-grid path data plus 4 aliases, registered through v0's
createTokens so a consumer can override a role, add one, or point a new
name at an existing glyph via createEmeraldPlugin({ icons }).

The set is seeded by promoting the dev showcase's hand-drawn art, which
was the only place this artwork existed. Deduping it turned up four
pairs of identical geometry, now modelled as aliases rather than copies:
contact/chat, orders/components, productivity/activity, envelope/mail.

EmIcon renders the resolved paths against the --emerald-icon-* scale,
which until now shipped as CSS variables nothing read. Stroke width is
set in CSS rather than as an attribute so a host class can restroke a
glyph without the component growing a prop for it. Icons stay out of the
accessibility tree unless given a label, which promotes them to
role=img. An unregistered role renders nothing and warns under __DEV__.

Refs #107

* refactor(emerald): render intrinsic glyphs through the icon system

The glyphs Em* components drew for themselves were inline SVG literals,
so a consumer overriding an icon role changed nothing about the system's
own chrome. They now resolve through EmIcon: EmCheckbox (check and
indeterminate marks), EmExpansionPanelCue, EmDialogClose,

* refactor(emerald): apply icon system QA fixes

The set shipped naming roles after the screen that first wanted them —
`dashboard` for a grid of rectangles, `logistics` for a truck — which is
the exact failure DESIGN_SYSTEMS.md §6 forbids, written by the same
change that introduced it. Twenty roles are renamed to what they draw
and every product name becomes an alias, so `dashboard` still resolves;
the census goes from 49 canonical / 4 aliases to 48 / 24. `finance` and
`payments` were two drawings of one card and are now one `card` role
with the better geometry, both names aliased to it. `kanban` and
`calendar` keep their names — those glyphs do depict the concept.

The dev pages move to canonical names rather than riding the aliases,
which meant splitting the shell's nav `id` in two: it was serving as
both route key and icon role, and that conflation is what the rename
exists to break. Item gains an explicit `icon`.

Also from review:
- The close buttons sized their hit area off `--emerald-icon-l/xl`. The
  icon scale measures glyphs; a 32px button that happens to match a
  token is a coincidence, so both take literals now.
- `EmeraldIconsOptions['icons']` takes glyphs only. It accepted a bare
  string too, which was a second, undocumented way to write an alias
  that could disagree with `aliases`.
- The fallback registry is now built only when injection actually
  misses, which is what its comment always claimed.
- `EmIconName` gives the `name` prop completion over both sets while
  still admitting consumer-registered roles.
- Tests follow the house `should` phrasing, assert the unknown-role
  warning fires exactly once, and cover two invariants the rename makes
  load-bearing: no alias shadows a canonical role, and overriding a
  shared target moves every alias pointing at it.
- Star path normalized to absolute coordinates and sort to explicit
  linetos; dead font-size/line-height dropped from both close buttons.

* refactor(emerald): make the icon system a standalone plugin

Icons were a branch of createEmeraldPlugin's install, which meant the
only way to get them was to take Emerald's theming with them. They are
now their own plugin built on v0's createPluginContext, with the three
option tiers the plugin family uses and a fallback factory so useEmIcons
still answers with the built-in set when nothing is installed.
createEmeraldPlugin composes it and `{ icons: false }` skips the install,
so the happy path is unchanged.

`src/icons.ts` splits: `icons/glyphs.ts` holds the artwork as a leaf
module with no imports, `icons/index.ts` holds the registry, plugin, and
consumer. There is no persist tier — the registry is built from static
artwork and never mutates, so there is no session state a reload could
lose.

The split was meant to let a consumer who skips icons drop the 1.9 kB
map. It does not, and the claim is retracted rather than shipped: a
module-scope trinity, `const [a, b, c] = createXContext()`, survives
tree-shaking in both rollup and esbuild even annotated /* @__PURE__ */.
Measured against the built dist, an entry importing a single colour
string still carries every glyph. The package already has two such
trinities in EmCalendar and EmKanban, so this predates the icon system
and is not something plugin composition can fix — a separate entry point
is the only mechanism that would. `{ icons: false }` is documented as a
registration switch, not a bundle switch, and the same caveat is
recorded in DESIGN_SYSTEMS.md so the next design system does not promise
what this one cannot deliver.

Nothing is lost by it in practice: seven Em* components import EmIcon, so
any app using Emerald's controls carries the map regardless of how the
plugin is installed.

chore(playground): add auto format for Vue files

Monaco has no formatter for .vue, so Format did nothing on App.vue.
Prettier now formats those files. An Auto format switch on the Format
item and in editor settings runs it when the editor blurs, and is off
by default so a blur rewrite cannot autosave a One playground.

The blur path writes the file that lost focus. vue-repl flushes editor
changes onto whichever file is active 250ms later, which would otherwise
paste the formatted text into the file you just switched to.

fix(play): compile package type imports in playground SFCs (#1002)

Vue's browser compiler rejects `import type` from a package inside
defineProps, defineEmits, and defineModel. Rewrite those imports to a
relative src/v0-macros.ts shim when an example loads, and keep the
shim out of the deletable file tree.
